title: Annotatio V §.IV FIRST genus (2)–(3): passion/death schema; Signatum known only to intellect
pass_a_gloss: (2) That Christ’s Body to be eaten in the Supper is to be eaten under its certain and definite schema — i.e. under the schema of the Passion and Death: For so Christ: This is my Body, which is broken for you and given unto death, Luke 22:19. Not which was born or nourished for you — although it is understood no less born and nourished for us than crucified and delivered unto death. So that the adversaries ridiculously mock the argument converting ‘which’ into ‘inasmuch as,’ unless they blaspheme that Christ Himself spoke ridiculously — i.e. made mention of His crucified Body without peculiar respect to this very thing. But under the schema of crucifixion and death Christ’s Body cannot be eaten Corporaliter and Oraliter, seeing that under this schema it is nowhere any longer corporally present (Rom. 6:9); But well Spiritualiter: so that we are therefore expressly commanded, as often as we eat of the bread which is sacramentally Christ’s Body, to recall the Lord’s death by memory — i.e. to turn it in the soul and make it known to others. (3) That Christ’s Body to be eaten in the Supper completes that part of the Supper’s Sacrament — consisting by the Sacrament’s nature of two parts, Sign and Signified — which they call the Signified, signified through the bread as Sign; But the nature of the Signified, according to Augustine, is that through a sign obvious to sense it becomes known to the intellect alone: But what is manifest to the intellect alone cannot be orally received and eaten, seeing that by that very act it would have to be exposed to sense and so far stripped of the signified’s nature.
pass_b_english: FIRST (2): it is to be eaten under the Passion/Death schema (‘broken for you / given unto death’) — not as merely born/nourished. Under crucifixion’s schema the Body is nowhere still corporally present (Rom. 6:9); it is well eaten spiritually, and we are told to remember the Lord’s death.
FIRST (3): as Signatum of the sacrament it is known to the intellect alone through the sense-sign (Augustine) — so it cannot be orally received without ceasing to be signified.
source_text: (2) Corpus Christi in Cœna manducandum, sub certo ac definito schemate suo, i. e. sub schemate Passionis & Mortis manducandum esse: Sic enim Christus: Hoc est Corpus meum, quod pro vobis frangitur & in mortem datur, Luc. 22, 19. Non quod pro vobis natum aut enutritum est, licèt non minùs pro nobis natum ac enutritum, quàm crucifixum & in mortem traditum intelligatur. Ut ridiculè irrideant adversarii argumentum, To quod, in quatenus convertens, nisi ipsum Christum ridiculè locutum, i. e. crucifixi Corporis sui mentionem, citra peculiarem in hoc ipsum respectum, blasphement fecisse. At sub crucifixionis mortisque schemate, Corpus Christi Corporaliter Oraliterque manducari non potest, utpote (sub hoc schemate nullibi ampliùs corporaliter præsens Rom. 6, 9.); Bene autem Spiritualiter: ut proinde jubeamur disertè, quotiescunque de pane, qui sacramentaliter Corpus Christi est, manducamus, mortem Domini memoriâ recolere, i. e. animâ volvere & aliis notam facere. (3) Corpus Christi in Cœna manducandum, Sacramenti Cœnæ, ex duabus partibus, per naturam Sacramenti, Signô scil. & Signato constantis, eam partem absolvere, quam Signatum vocant, per panem ceu Signum significatum; At Significati ea natura est, juxta Augustinum, ut per signum sensui obvium, soli intellectui innotescat: Quod verò soli intellectui manifestum sit, id oraliter accipi ac manducari non potest, utpote hôc ipsô sensui exponendum, atque eatenus signati naturâ exuendum.
